newsitem.title: ITALY: Olivetti brings in auto parts group boss as chief.
newsitem.headline: Olivetti brings in auto parts group boss as chief.

text.p: Italian information technology group Olivetti has turned to a man who helped build a car components empire to retool its ailing business after summarily dismissing chief executive officer Francesco Caio.

An emergency board meeting on Wednesday evening brought Caio's 73-day rein at the helm of the crisis-hit group to a sudden end. Roberto Colaninno, who currently runs auto components group Sogefi, was appointed to succeed him.
Caio's replacement by Colaninno, 53, is the latest twist in a chain of events following Carlo De Benedetti's resignation from the Olivetti board on September 3 after 18 years as group chairman.

Panic-selling on the Milan stock exchange has wiped nearly 40 percent off the loss-making company's market capitalisation since De Benedetti's dramatic exit and after doubts were cast over the accuracy of Olivetti's financial accounts.

Colaninno is seen as enjoying the confidence of De Benedetti, who remains Olivetti's largest shareholder with a 15 percent stake. De Benedetti's industrial holding company CIR also controls Sogefi, founded by Colaninno in 1981.
Some analysts had said in advance of the board meeting that they hoped that someone with a strong background in telecommunications would take the helm at Olivetti.
"People are not going to be happy with someone who is not from the telecoms industry," said Marie-Christine Keith at James Capel in London. "Investors want someone who knows the business."
Olivetti is investing heavily in telecommunications ventures although its core businesses are still office equipment, systems integration and personal computers.

In Milan, an analyst who has closely followed the company's declining fortunes for a number of years, said Colaninno appeared to be someone who could reassure Olivetti's bankers who are thought to be nervous about the group's mounting woes.
"You can see Colaninno as an expression of the bank environment who De Benedetti is also happy with," said the analyst who requested anonymity.
Colaninno sits on the board of two banks, Banca Agricola Mantovana and Banca Steinhauslin.
Others speculated that Colaninno may be a stop-gap figure who will run Olivetti while the search goes on for a prominent figure in the telecommunications industry to take over.

Former chairman De Benedetti was reported to be the prime mover behind the ouster of Caio, his former assistant who master-minded the launch last year of Olivetti's 41.3 percent owned Omnitel mobile phone venture.
The upheavals have seen Olivetti shares plunge to record lows as investors dumped the stock as concerns mounted over what the loss-making group's real financial state was.
The company side-stepped key questions about its business put by market regulators by issuing a statement early Wednesday giving details of some of its affairs but leaving out others.

When the stock opened Wednesday it rebounded from record lows of 465 lire set on Tuesday and triggered automatic suspension by touching a 10 percent trading ceiling and forging a day's high of 511.5 lire ($0.335). It then failed to resume trade.

Caio, 39, Tesone and De Benedetti are being investigated by magistrates in Olivetti's home town of Ivrea in north west Italy who suspect the company may have issued misleading statements about its financial position, judicial sources say. ($1=1527 Lire)
